site: Taronga Western Plains Zoo, Dubbo, NSW, Australia
method: GPS coordinates remain source-graded. Existing finite coordinates are OpenStreetMap community animal-attraction points and may be approximate, outdated, or inside habitats rather than public viewing positions. All 36 exact supplied zoo JPEG copies currently tracked in data/observations.json were audited for EXIF: none retains EXIF, GPS or capture timestamps. Therefore photographs are used only as animal/exhibit evidence, never converted into invented latitude/longitude. Official Taronga map-grid references remain non-GPS until a reliable coordinate source or an explicitly saved on-site viewing position exists.

points.name: Giraffes · northern paddock
points.fact: Giraffes have remarkable circulation systems that help supply blood to their brains despite their height.
points.prompt: Look for individual coat-pattern shapes. Each giraffe has a distinctive pattern, but matching an animal to a name needs keeper records.

points.name: Giraffes · southern paddock
points.fact: Giraffes use a long, prehensile tongue and flexible lips to browse trees.
points.prompt: Can you see browsing versus simply standing? Don't assume every giraffe you see has the same name or lineage.
points.officialMapRef: Giraffe visitor area 14F (current web itinerary; this OSM point is not claimed as the photo camera position)

points.name: Zebras · Gateway paddock
points.fact: Zebra stripes vary between individuals and may help reduce biting-fly landings in some settings.
points.prompt: Notice how the stripes continue across the legs and shoulders. Patterns can help identify individuals with verified photos.

points.name: Zebras · savannah paddock
points.fact: Wild zebras live with complex social relationships and use body posture, sound and smell to communicate.
points.prompt: Try watching whether two zebras stay close or take turns moving — without guessing why from a single moment.

points.name: Common hippopotamus
points.fact: Hippos spend much of the day in or near water, but they feed mainly on land.
points.prompt: Check what is directly visible above the waterline. A submerged hippo can be hard to count.

points.name: Eastern bongo
points.fact: Bongos are forest antelopes with striking vertical stripes that help break up their outline among vegetation.
points.prompt: Can you spot the ears before the body? A stripe is a camouflage feature, not proof of an animal's sex.

points.name: Common eland
points.fact: Eland are among the world's largest antelopes and can move with surprising agility.
points.prompt: Compare the body shape and horns with other antelopes nearby. What can you identify confidently?

points.name: White rhinoceros
points.fact: The white rhino's broad lips suit grazing. Its name does not mean it must be white in colour.
points.prompt: Watch how the muzzle comes close to grass. Contrast a grazer's lip shape with browsing black rhinos.

points.name: Black rhinoceros
points.fact: Black rhinos have an upper lip that helps grasp leaves and twigs.
points.prompt: See whether it browses branches instead of short grass. Keep a respectful distance and never feed wildlife.

points.name: Siamangs · Wild Asia
points.fact: Siamangs move through trees using long arms; they also have a throat sac used in powerful calls.
points.prompt: Listen for a duet if the animals are calling; silence is also normal. The keeper video records real siamang sounds.

points.name: Small-clawed otters
points.fact: Asian small-clawed otters use their sensitive front paws to explore food and surfaces.
points.prompt: Look for paw movements near the water rather than assuming a particular activity without seeing it.

points.name: Sumatran tigers · Wild Asia east
points.fact: Sumatran tigers are forest-adapted predators, and individuals can be difficult to spot among dense vegetation.
points.prompt: What colours and shapes blend into the foliage? A hidden tiger does not mean the exhibit is empty.

points.name: Sumatran tigers · Wild Asia west
points.fact: A tiger's stripe pattern is individual, but a distant visitor photo does not prove which named tiger is visible.
points.prompt: Notice the difference between observing an animal and knowing its identity.

points.name: Ring-tailed lemurs
points.fact: Ring-tailed lemurs use their long striped tails in visual communication and balance.
points.prompt: Count how many are clearly visible; don't assume you have counted the entire group.

points.name: Fallow deer
points.fact: Fallow deer are highly variable in colour, even within one species.
points.prompt: Can you distinguish body markings from shadow in the trees?

points.name: Addax · Waterhole area
points.fact: Addax are desert-adapted antelopes, with broad hooves that help when moving over sandy ground.
points.prompt: Look for their distinctive spiral horns and where their hooves contact the ground.

points.name: Asian elephants
points.fact: Asian elephants use trunk whiskers and sensitive skin to examine objects. Recent research reveals just how specialised these structures are.
points.prompt: Watch what the trunk touches, but don't infer the elephant's identity or intention from a still.
points.sourceType: Current Taronga map-grid references + photo-backed field observation; GPS not verified

points.name: African wild dogs
points.fact: Wild dogs have complex pack cooperation, but the number visible from a path is not a full pack count.
points.prompt: Notice markings, direction of travel and interactions rather than naming an individual without confirmation.
points.sourceType: Current Taronga map-grid reference + photo-backed field observation; GPS not verified

points.name: Meerkats · The Waterhole
points.fact: Meerkats live in social groups and take turns watching for danger, but standing upright does not by itself identify the duty an individual has.
points.prompt: Can you see more than one animal using different positions?
points.sourceType: Current Taronga Waterhole/map-grid context + photo-backed probable-meerkat observation; GPS not verified

points.name: Galápagos giant tortoises
points.fact: Galápagos giant tortoises belong to different island lineages; shell shape alone cannot confirm an individual animal's origin.
points.prompt: Look at the shell, feet and head and describe what is visible before guessing age or sex.
points.sourceType: Current Taronga map-grid reference + photo-backed field observation; GPS not verified

points.name: African lions · Pride Lands
points.mapRef: Lion Pride Lands 19R; secondary African Adventure view 17P
points.fact: Lions often rest for long periods, especially in warm weather. The whole pride may not be visible at once.
points.prompt: How many lions can you actually see, and how many might be behind vegetation?
points.sourceType: Current Taronga Lion Pride Lands/map-grid references + photo-backed field observation; GPS not verified

points.name: Cheetahs
points.fact: Cheetahs are built for acceleration, with a flexible spine and long legs.
points.prompt: Can you spot the dark facial tear marks? Remember their exhibit space is not a racing track.
points.sourceType: Current Taronga map-grid reference; GPS not verified

points.name: Greater one-horned rhinoceroses
points.fact: The folds of one-horned rhino skin can resemble armour plates, but the skin is living, sensitive tissue.
points.prompt: Compare its single horn and body folds with the African rhinoceroses.
points.sourceType: Current Taronga map-grid references; GPS not verified

photoGeodataAudit.conclusion: No embedded camera geodata survived in any of the 36 exact supplied JPEG copies. Photo sets support animal/exhibit context only; they do not independently verify a GPS pin.
photoGeodataAudit.method: Matched observation filenames and byte sizes to exact Library JPEG copies, then inspected raw JPEG EXIF/GPS metadata.
